Assuming the ratio of post baseline UPCR over baseline UPCR follows a lognormal distribution, the
primary endpoint of relative decrease in UPCR will be estimated based on an MMRM (mixed effects
model for repeated measure) model. In this model, the ratio of post baseline UPCR over baseline
UPCR at month 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, and 24 in log scale will be response variable, while baseline UPCR in
log scale, treatment, visit, treatment by visit interaction will be fixed effect covariates. Within group
treatment effect estimates and between group treatments comparisons will be based on this MMRM
model. Unstructured covariance structure will be the default method, if model cannot converge,
compound symmetry covariance structure will be used. For within group comparison, estimates on
relative decrease from baseline and associated standard error will be displayed. For between groups,
the geometric mean ratio of UPCR at post baseline over baseline between treatment group vs placebo
group, its associated
 and confidence intervals will be provided as well.


If the MMRM model still run into convergence issues after changing covariance structure, we will
impute missing values with the "last observation carried forward" method and use an ANCOVA
model to perform related analysis by each post baseline visit. In this case, baseline log UPCR and
treatment group will serve as covariates.
In addition, the raw UPCR values will be summarized descriptively by treatment and visit.

Endpoints and assessments
The primary endpoint was the change from baseline in
24-hour urine protein:creatinine ratio (UPCR) at 9 months.
Secondary endpoints included change in eGFR and the inci-
dence and severity of treatment-emergent AEs. Exploratory
endpoints included change from baseline in Gd-IgA1 and
polyclonal IgA, IgG, and IgM. Proteinuria (24-hour UPCR)
and eGFR were assessed at screening, predose at baseline, and
at months 3, 6 (end of treatment [EOT]), 9, 12, 15, 18, 21,
and 24 (end of study). Serum Gd-IgA1 was measured using a
validated
electrochemiluminescence
assay
(MorphoSys
GmbH), and serum IgM, IgG, and IgA were measured using
immunoturbidimetric assays (Roche) at baseline and on days
8, 15, 22, 29, 57, 85 (3 months), 113, 141, 169 (6 months;
EOT), 267 (9 months), 366 (12 months), 457 (15 months),
548 (18 months), 639 (21 months), and 730 (24 months; end
of study). Assessments were performed through 12 months in
part 2. Safety monitoring included vital signs, physical ex-
aminations, electrocardiograms, hematology and chemistry,
coagulation, and urinalysis. All AEs were recorded and graded
using Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events,
version 5.0.
Statistical analysis
Sample size was determined without formal hypothesis
testing or type I error considerations. Part 1 was planned with
a target enrollment of 11 patients per treatment arm, which
with an assumed dropout rate of 10% would result in 10
patients per treatment arm. For part 2, a total of 8 Japanese
patients were estimated to be sufficient for open-label
observations.
Patients, investigators, and clinic site and study personnel
were blinded to treatment in part 1; part 2 was open-label.
The site pharmacist was unblinded to manage study drug
preparation. Sponsor personnel responsible for the pre-
specified 9-month UPCR primary analysis were unblinded on
April 25, 2023. No unblinded patient data were provided to
clinical sites before the final database lock. The final 24-
month analysis was performed on August 9, 2024.
Efficacy analyses were performed using the per protocol set
(PPS; patients who met PPS criteria for minimum exposure
and use of prohibited therapy; part 1, n 1⁄4 41; part 2, n 1⁄4 6).
Seven patients in part 1 (2-dose, n 1⁄4 1; 5-dose, n 1⁄4 3; and 9-
dose, n 1⁄4 3) were excluded from the PPS for receiving #3
infusions of blinded study drug. Three additional patients
received prohibited therapy and remained in the PPS until the
time of prohibited medication. Safety analyses included pa-
tients who received $1 dose of study treatment (full analysis
set; n 1⁄4 54) grouped by actual treatment. Pharmacodynamic
analyses included patients in the PPS with $1 available sample.
Continuous variables were summarized using means, SD,
medians, and interquartile ranges. Categorical variables were
summarized using numbers and proportions of patients.
Time to serum Ig recovery (first measurement within 10% of
baseline following on-treatment nadir) was estimated using
the
Kaplan-Meier
time-to-event
analysis.
Patients
were
censored at the time of study discontinuation and initiation of
prohibited therapy. The primary endpoint (decrease in 24-
hour UPCR) was estimated using a mixed-effects model
with repeated measures, in which the percentage change from
baseline in UPCR was the response variable and baseline
UPCR, treatment, visit, and treatment by visit interaction
were fixed-effect covariates. The model made no assumptions
for correlation of UPCR between visits within a patient.
Within-group treatment comparisons were summarized using
least-squares means and standard error derived from the
mixed-effects model with repeated measures. The change
from baseline in eGFR was assessed using the mixed-effects
model with repeated measures on the additive scale.
Missing values were not imputed but were handled via the
mixed-effects model with repeated measures missing-at-
random assumption. Analyses were performed using SAS
version 9.4 or higher (SAS Institute).

Guidelines for the treatment of IgAN recommend renin-

and prevent progression to kidney failure, as well as sup-

because RAS blockade does not address the underlying
pathogenesis of IgAN, many patients with IgAN have

Recently

pathogenic IgA through B/plasma cell modulation, predom-

tory pathways in the kidneys, but it is unclear how they will
impact the standard of care.20 Thus, there remains an unmet
need for treatments that target the proximal causes of IgAN
and have sustained effects after treatment is discontinued.
Inhibiting the production of Gd-IgA1 and anti-Gd-IgA1
through depletion of early CD20þ B-cell lineages with rit-
uximab has been shown to be ineffective for improving
proteinuria and maintaining kidney function in IgAN.21
However, targeting CD38, which is highly expressed by
mature antibody-secreting plasma cells and plasmablasts,22-27
is a potential therapeutic approach for IgAN. Felzartamab is
an investigational, fully human IgG1 monoclonal anti-CD38
antibody
that

Clinical
studies have demonstrated that felzartamab has an acceptable
safety profile with preliminary evidence of efficacy in the
treatment of primary membranous nephropathy, antibody-
mediated rejection, and multiple myeloma.34-36 IGNAZ is a
randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2a study
that assessed the efficacy and safety of felzartamab in patients
with IgAN and persistent proteinuria despite RAS blockade.
METHODS
Study design and oversight
IGNAZ (ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05065970) is a randomized,
double-blind, multicenter, placebo-controlled phase 2a study
that enrolled patients at 33 centers in the Czech Republic,
Japan, Spain, Republic of Korea, Germany, Serbia, Bulgaria,
Georgia, Ukraine, Belgium, the Philippines, the United States,
Malaysia, and Taiwan. The study was conducted in 2 parts,
each with a screening period, 6-month treatment period, and
follow-up period (part 1, 18 months; part 2, 6 months;
Supplementary Figure S1).
IGNAZ was conducted in accordance with the ICH
Harmonized Tripartite Guidelines for Good Clinical Practice,
Declaration of Helsinki, and Council for International Or-
ganizations of Medical Sciences International Ethical Guide-
lines. The study protocol was approved by the ethical review
committees and institutional review boards at each site. Pa-
tients provided written, informed consent.
Randomization and treatment
In part 1, patients were randomized 1:1:1:1 in permuted
blocks by interactive response technology to receive 9 i.v.
infusions of placebo or felzartamab in 1 of 3 arms (2-dose, 5-
dose, or 9-dose) by body weight (#50 kg, 650 mg; >50-70
kg, 975 mg; >70-90 kg, 1300 mg; and >90 kg, 1625 mg) on
days 1, 8, 15, 22, 29, 57, 85, 113, and 141 (Supplementary
Figure S1). Planned enrollment in part 1 was 44 patients
(11 per arm). After 48 patients were randomized in part 1, 6
Japanese patients were enrolled in part 2 and received the
felzartamab 9-dose schedule open-label. Patients received
standard of care with an angiotensin-converting enzyme in-
hibitor and/or angiotensin receptor blocker throughout the
study. Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors could be
continued but not initiated. Systemic immunosuppressive
therapies were prohibited for more than 7 consecutive days
within 180 days before signing informed consent.
Patients were monitored for infusion-related reactions
(IRRs) for $2 hours after the first 3 infusions and $1 hour
after all infusions that followed an IRR. Before the first 3
infusions, all patients were to receive oral paracetamol
(acetaminophen) 650-1000 mg, oral/i.v. diphenhydramine
50 mg (or equivalent), histamine type 2 receptor antagonists
(e.g., i.v. famotidine 20 mg or equivalent), and i.v. methyl-
prednisolone 50-100 mg (or equivalent). If no IRRs occurred
during the first infusion, the infusion speed could be
increased from 2 ml/min to 4 ml/min (second infusion) or
8 ml/min (subsequent infusions).
Felzartamab was withheld for active infection requiring
systemic therapy or any grade $3 adverse event (AE) until
resolution to grade #2. Infusions were stopped for grade $2
IRR or allergic reaction or grade 1 cytokine release syndrome

discontinued for grade $3 IRR or allergic reaction or
grade $2 cytokine release syndrome, grade 4 serious AE due
to treatment-related infection, intolerable toxicity, or with-
drawal of consent.

EFFICACY ANALYSIS
All efficacy endpoints will be analysed by treatment arm using the FAS. Sensitivity analysis of
selected efficacy endpoints may be performed on PPS as needed.
Patients enrolled in double-blind Part I of the study will undergo secondary and

7.1
Urine protein to creatinine ratio (UPCR)
The baseline of 24h UPCR is defined as the mean of the values determined at screening and prior to
baseline (visit 2) predose (UPCR from 24h urine).
Assuming the ratio of post baseline UPCR over baseline UPCR follows a lognormal distribution, the
primary endpoint of relative decrease in UPCR will be estimated based on an MMRM (mixed effects
model for repeated measure) model. In this model, the ratio of post baseline UPCR over baseline
UPCR at month 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, and 24 in log scale will be response variable, while baseline UPCR in
log scale, treatment, visit, treatment by visit interaction will be fixed effect covariates. Within group
treatment effect estimates and between group treatments comparisons will be based on this MMRM
model. Unstructured covariance structure will be the default method, if model cannot converge,
compound symmetry covariance structure will be used. For within group comparison, estimates on
relative decrease from baseline and associated standard error will be displayed. For between groups,
the geometric mean ratio of UPCR at post baseline over baseline between treatment group vs placebo
group, its associated
 and confidence intervals will be provided as well.


If the MMRM model still run into convergence issues after changing covariance structure, we will
impute missing values with the "last observation carried forward" method and use an ANCOVA
model to perform related analysis by each post baseline visit. In this case, baseline log UPCR and
treatment group will serve as covariates.
In addition, the raw UPCR values will be summarized descriptively by treatment and visit.

The Global Study: Part I is a randomized, double-blind clinical trial. The patient, investigator,
clinical site staff, sponsor and the entire clinical study processing team will remain blinded to
treatment assignment. Only site staff (pharmacist and/or other appropriate qualified staff) who
manage IMP will be unblinded to enable IMP preparation according to the patient's assigned
randomization number. The placebo in this study will be infusion of 0.9% sodium infusion solution.

Clinical Research Organization (CRO) Medical Monitor or the sponsor, whenever possible.
However, the responsibility to break the treatment code in an emergency resides solely with the
investigator.
If the investigator breaks the blind during the course of the clinical trial, the patient must
discontinue the trial treatment (see Section 8.1). Time and reason for breaking the blind will be
documented in the eCRF.
Unblinding of suspected unexpected serious adverse reactions (SUSARs) and distribution of

will be outlined in the Safety Management Plan (SMP) for the trial, including the description of

Any analysis and aggregate reporting of unblinded data before the database lock for the primary
analysis and unblinding of the trial will be performed according to the SMP or Statistical Analysis
Plan (SAP) or PK/
Data Analysis Plan by a separate team from the trial. No unblinded patient

Abstract
Introduction: Felzartamab is a fully human anti-CD38
monoclonal antibody under investigation for treatment of
IgA nephropathy (IgAN). IGNAZ (NCT05065970) is a
randomized, double blind, placebo-controlled Phase 2a study
that assessed the efficacy and safety of felzartamab in 54
patients with biopsy-confirmed IgAN despite maximal renin
angiotensin system blockade.
Methods: In part 1, patients were randomized in the 6-
month treatment period to receive intravenous placebo (12
patients) or felzartamab in three arms: two doses in 15 days
(2-dose, 12 patients), five doses in 2 months (5-dose, 11
patients), or nine doses in five months (9-dose, 13 patients).
In part 2, six Japanese patients received the felzartamab 9-
dose schedule open-label. Follow-up in parts 1 and 2 was 24
and 12 months, respectively, after the first dose. The primary
endpoint was change in proteinuria (urine protein to
creatinine ratio [UPCR]) at nine months.
Results: Treatment with felzartamab versus placebo led to
rapid (within 3-6 months) reduction in least-squares mean
UPCR sustained at nine months (placebo, -5.7%; 2-dose,
-12.5%; 5-dose, -12.8%; 9-dose, -29.5%; part 2, -44.8%) and
at 18 months after ending treatment (24 months), particularly
in the 9-dose arm (-44.5%). Mean decreases in estimated
glomerular filtration rate were lower with felzartamab than
with placebo through 24 months in part 1 and 12 months in
part 2. Felzartamab safety was consistent with prior
observations; adverse events were predominantly grade 1
or 2.
Conclusions: Treatment with felzartamab results in
sustained reduction of proteinuria, suggesting disease
improvement. Further evidence is needed to understand the
impact of felzartamab on preservation of kidney function in
high-risk patients with IgAN.

IgA nephropathy is the most common primary glomer-
ular disease worldwide, leading to kidney failure in a
large proportion of patients. Despite the standard of care
that includes renin-angiotensin blockade, many patients
with IgA nephropathy (IgAN) will experience persistent
proteinuria and progressive loss of kidney function, ul-
timately resulting in poor outcomes. Targeting the un-
derlying pathogenic events in IgAN is an essential
component of an optimal treatment strategy. Thus, a
potential therapeutic approach is to deplete CD38þ

IgAN. In the IGNAZ phase 2a study, treatment with fel-

modulate the underlying pathogenesis of IgAN.

the

time-to-event
analysis.

were
censored at the time of study discontinuation and initiation of

least-squares means and standard error derived from the
mixed-effects model with repeated measures. The change
from baseline in eGFR was assessed using the mixed-effects
model with repeated measures on the additive scale.

mixed-effects model with repeated measures missing-at-
random assumption. Analyses were performed using SAS
version 9.4 or higher (SAS Institute).
